The oldest lighthouse of which there is a substantial record stood on the island of Pharos, at the entrance to the harbor of Alexandria in Egypt. Built in the third century BCE, probably during the reign of Ptolemy II, it rose in several stages to a height that ancient writers put at roughly 100 meters, and a fire burned at its top, reflected outward by polished metal. The tower was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and its name gave the rest of the world a word for the thing. In Greek, the island was Pharos, and the Romans and Italians kept the root, so that the Italian *faro* and the French *phare* both descend from a single Egyptian islet. The structure survived for well over a millennium, damaged by earthquakes, and its ruins finally disappeared into the sea in the medieval period. Its importance lies less in its shape than in the idea it established: that a fixed point of light could turn a dangerous coast into a navigable one.

The Romans understood the same principle and built on it across their empire. The Tower of Hercules at A Coruña, on the northwestern coast of Spain, was raised in the first or second century CE and, after later restoration, still stands and still guides ships, which makes it the oldest lighthouse in continuous use. Roman harbors such as Ostia near the mouth of the Tiber and Dover on the English Channel had their own towers, and a few of their stone foundations survive. The Roman system depended on a dense network of ports, roads and garrisons, and when that network decayed after the fall of the western empire, the knowledge of how to maintain such structures went with it. For several centuries the coasts of Europe were lit, if at all, by bonfires lit on headlands and by the occasional tower maintained by a religious house or a town.

The medieval revival was slow and largely practical. Lighthouses appeared where trade justified the expense: at the approaches to busy ports, on dangerous headlands, and at crossings where pilgrims and merchants depended on safe passage. The Lanterna at Genoa, first recorded in the twelfth century, became a model for the Italian tradition, and the tower at Hook Head on the southeast coast of Ireland, traditionally dated to the same period, is often cited as one of the oldest lights still operating in the British Isles. Many of these early lights were not owned by governments at all. They were founded by monasteries, funded by tolls on passing shipping, or maintained by private guilds, and the right to collect dues was often more valuable to the owner than the light itself. In England, the corporation known as Trinity House received its royal charter in 1514 and gradually acquired responsibility for lights along the coast, and it remains an important authority to this day.

The fundamental difficulty with early lighthouses was that the light itself was weak. Open fires, burning coal or wood or tallow, gave a flame that smoked, flickered, and was hard to distinguish from the glow of a town or another ship. Keeping such a fire burning through a storm required constant attention, and the tower was exposed to the same weather that made it necessary. Improvement came in stages. Oil lamps replaced open hearths, and in the late eighteenth century the Swiss-born inventor Aimé Argand developed a lamp with a tubular wick and a glass chimney that produced a brighter and steadier flame. Reflectors, usually curved metal or silvered glass mirrors placed behind each lamp, concentrated that light into a beam that could be seen much farther away. The combination was a real advance, but it still had limits, because the reflectors gathered only a portion of the light the lamp produced and threw it in a broad, unfocused pattern.

The more dramatic problem was architectural. The coasts that most needed lights were often the coasts with the most dangerous rocks offshore, and building a tower on a reef that is submerged for much of each day is a formidable task. The history of British lighthouse engineering is largely a history of attempts to solve this. In 1698 Henry Winstanley, a London engineer and eccentric, completed a timber lighthouse on the Eddystone Rock, several miles off Plymouth, but the structure was swept away in a storm in 1703, taking Winstanley with it. A successor built by John Rudyerd, also of wood, lasted until a fire destroyed it in 1755. The engineer John Smeaton then designed a tower of granite blocks, dovetailed and bonded with a hydraulic lime that set underwater, and his structure, completed in 1759, stood for over a century. The stones were dismantled in 1877, when the rock beneath them had been eroded, and the tower was rebuilt on Plymouth Hoe, where it remains as a monument. Smeaton's method, which treated the lighthouse as a single interlocked mass of masonry designed to resist the sea rather than merely endure it, became the template for offshore construction.

The Bell Rock, a reef in the North Sea off the coast of Scotland, presented an even more formidable challenge. It lies submerged at most states of the tide, and for years the Northern Lighthouse Board had been unable to find a way to build on it. The engineer Robert Stevenson, grandfather of the novelist Robert Louis Stevenson, oversaw the construction of a tower between 1807 and 1810. Workers lived in a floating barracks, and they landed on the rock only during the brief periods of low water, cutting the sandstone and fitting it into place with a precision that the sea could not undo. The light was first exhibited in 1811 and is still in service. The Stevenson family went on to build many of Scotland's lighthouses, and their accumulated knowledge, recorded in journals and reports, formed a practical body of engineering that other nations would borrow.

The greatest single advance in the optics of lighthouses came from France. Augustin-Jean Fresnel, a physicist trained in the study of light as a wave, realized that a large lens could be built from a series of concentric prismatic rings, each bending the light into a parallel beam while using far less glass than a solid lens of the same focal power. The Fresnel lens was first installed at the Cordouan light at the mouth of the Gironde in 1823, and it transformed the performance of the coast. A single lamp inside a lens of this kind could throw a beam many tens of kilometers, far beyond the range of any reflector system. Lenses were graded into orders according to size, and the largest, the first order, could be several meters tall and weigh several tons. Their rotation, driven by clockwork and later by electric motors, created a characteristic pattern of flashes, so that each lighthouse had a signature that a navigator could identify from its rhythm alone. This was not a decorative detail. A sailor approaching an unfamiliar coast at night, trying to match the lights on his chart to the lights on the horizon, needed a way to tell one from another, and the flash pattern became the means.

Lighthouses also became institutions. Governments that had once left the work to private owners took it over in the nineteenth century, partly because maritime trade had become too important to leave to chance and partly because the expense of building proper lights was beyond most private investors. In the United States, the Lighthouse Act of 1789 placed the nation's lights under federal control, a decision made early in the life of the republic. Boston Light, on Little Brewster Island at the entrance to Boston Harbor, had been first lit in 1716 by the colonial government of Massachusetts and was rebuilt after the Revolution; it remains the oldest lighthouse site in the country. Portland Head Light in Maine, completed in 1791, was another early federal station. The keepers who tended these lights were often poorly paid, isolated, and subject to the political whims of the authorities who employed them, and their lives produced a literature of memoirs and oral histories that complements the engineering record. Many keepers lived with their families on the rock or headland, and the rhythm of their days was set by the need to trim wicks, polish lenses, and wind the clockwork that turned the light through the night.

The twentieth century brought electricity, and with it a long process of automation. Electric arc lamps and then incandescent bulbs replaced oil, and motors replaced clockwork. Radio beacons and fog signals supplemented the visual light, and eventually the light itself was no longer the only means by which ships found their way. Satellite navigation has since made the lighthouse less essential to the working mariner, though it has not made it obsolete. Lights are still maintained as aids to navigation, as backups against electronic failure, and as landmarks, and many have been preserved as museums or as protected historic structures. The keepers, once a distinct profession, have largely disappeared, replaced by remote monitoring and periodic maintenance crews, and the change has been mourned by many who grew up in lighthouse communities.

Looking back across two thousand years, what is striking is how little the basic purpose has changed. The Pharos of Alexandria, the Tower of Hercules, the wooden structures of Winstanley and the granite tower of Smeaton were all attempts to answer the same question: how to make a coast visible to someone who cannot see it and who may be drowning in the attempt. The answers have moved from fire to oil to electric light, from reflectors to lenses, from wood to stone to reinforced concrete and steel, and from keepers to automated systems. Yet the lighthouse remains a fixed point in an uncertain world, a sign that someone, at some time, decided that the dangers of a particular stretch of water were worth the effort of marking. Its history is in large part the history of that decision, repeated by one generation after another, on coasts that were never quite safe and never quite forgotten.

The lighthouse is among the oldest of human engineering projects, and its history is mostly a history of fire. For most of its life, a lighthouse was a platform on which someone burned wood, coal, oil, or gas high enough to be seen from a ship at sea, and the story of the lighthouse is the story of making that flame brighter, steadier, easier to tell from other lights, and less dependent on human labor. The most famous early example was the Pharos of Alexandria, built on the small island of Pharos at the entrance to the harbor, probably in the reign of Ptolemy II in the third century BC. The ancient writer Lucian credited its design to Sostratus of Cnidus, and later accounts describe a stone tower of several stages, perhaps over a hundred metres tall, with a fire burning at the top. Some ancient sources suggest that polished metal or glass was used to concentrate the light, though this is uncertain. The tower survived for well over a thousand years before earthquakes damaged it in the fourteenth century. Its name became the word for lighthouse in several languages, including the Italian *faro* and the Spanish *faro*, and it remained the model that later builders had in mind.

Between the fall of Rome and the revival of maritime trade in the Middle Ages, lighthouses appear less often in the historical record, but they did not disappear. The Tower of Hercules at A Coruña, on the northwest coast of Spain, was built by the Romans in the first or second century AD and has been in continuous use ever since, making it the oldest surviving lighthouse still operating. It was restored in later centuries, and its present appearance reflects many rebuildings, yet its core is ancient. Other medieval towers were built on coasts and river mouths in Italy, France, and the Low Countries, often by religious houses, port authorities, or town corporations. These lights were commonly financed by dues levied on ships, a practice that would persist for centuries. A lighthouse was expensive to build and keep lit, so its existence depended on whoever collected revenue from the traffic it served.

Fire itself was the main limitation. A coal or wood fire gave off smoke, needed constant tending, and was exposed to wind and rain. Lanterns with glass panes protected the flame, but glass was dim and absorbed light, and the iron or wooden frames that held it cast shadows. Early lighthouses could be recognized mainly by their position and their height, not by any distinctive pattern of light. Mariners relied on landmarks, charts, and soundings, and a light was useful chiefly as a warning that land was near. Improvement came slowly, through better fuel, better lamps, and better placement, and the engineers who worked on these problems were often men with other trades, such as clockmakers, instrument makers, and military engineers.

The eighteenth century brought two changes that made the modern lighthouse possible. The first was engineering on difficult sites. Rocks that were submerged at high tide, or lay far out in open water, had long been dangerous, and building a tower on them seemed impossible. In 1698 Henry Winstanley completed a wooden lighthouse on the Eddystone Rock, off Plymouth in England, but it was swept away in a storm in 1703, along with its builder. John Smeaton, a civil engineer, designed the next Eddystone tower in the 1750s. He used a hydraulic lime mortar that set under water, and he shaped the granite blocks so that each course interlocked with the one beneath it, in a form he compared to the trunk of an oak. The tower, completed in 1759, stood for more than a century before its failing rock foundation forced its replacement. Smeaton's principles of stone construction and interlocking courses influenced lighthouse design for generations. In Scotland, Robert Stevenson built a tower on the Bell Rock, a reef twelve miles off the coast of Angus, between 1807 and 1810, working from a floating base and landing crews only during brief windows of calm water. The Stevenson family went on to build many of the lights around the coasts of Scotland, and their work set a standard for remote-site engineering.

The second change was optical. In the 1780s the Swiss physicist Aimé Argand developed a lamp with a hollow circular wick and a glass chimney, which produced a much brighter and steadier flame than the older open lamps. Lamps like this, fed by oil and fitted with reflectors, were widely adopted in the early nineteenth century. Reflectors, typically parabolic mirrors of silvered copper or glass, concentrated the light into a beam, but they were heavy, fragile, and lost efficiency as the silvering tarnished. The decisive advance came with the French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel, who in the 1820s designed a lens built from concentric prismatic rings. Each ring bent light passing through it toward the horizon, so that a lamp at the focus of the lens could throw its light in a powerful, narrow beam while using far less glass than a solid lens of the same effect. Fresnel's first large lens was installed at the Cordouan lighthouse at the mouth of the Gironde in 1823, and the design spread quickly through France and then to Britain and elsewhere. Lenses were classified into orders, from the great first-order lenses that stood several metres tall to small lenses for harbor lights, and the arrangement of their panels could be used to give each light a distinct character.

Because many lights looked alike from a distance, the ability to distinguish one light from another became essential. Mariners who saw a fixed white light could not tell whether they were looking at a headland or a harbor or a reef. Engineers therefore developed flashing lights, revolving lenses, and the grouping of flashes, each pattern timed so that a navigator with a chart and a watch could identify the station. Revolving apparatus was driven first by weights, like a clock, and later by clockwork and eventually by electric motors. Lamps progressed from oil to paraffin vapour, then to incandescent burners, and by the late nineteenth century to electric arc lamps and, in some cases, gas. Every new light source required new mechanisms, and the lighthouse became an assembly of optics, clockwork, and fuel management, all of which needed skilled maintenance.

Governance followed the technology. In Britain, Trinity House in London and the Northern Lighthouse Board in Edinburgh managed coastal lights and were funded by dues on shipping. In the United States, the federal government took responsibility for lighthouses from the early republic onward, with Boston Light, first lit in 1716 and rebuilt after the British destroyed it during the Revolutionary War, among the earliest of its stations. Congress created the Lighthouse Board in 1852, and in 1939 the Lighthouse Service was merged into the Coast Guard. Each country built networks of lights, lightships anchored where no tower could stand, and fog signals in the form of bells, whistles, and sirens to warn when visibility failed. The lighthouse keeper became a familiar figure, living on remote stations with his family, maintaining the lamp and lens, logging weather and passing ships, and often rescuing sailors from wrecks. Their lives were hard and isolated, and the stories of keepers, including famous rescues and long storm vigils, became part of the cultural memory of the coast.

The twentieth century brought the gradual end of the manned lighthouse. Electricity made lamps easier to run, and radio navigation, and later satellite positioning, reduced the dependence of ships on fixed visual aids. Automatic lamps with timing devices and remote monitoring spread from the 1920s onward, and many stations were automated over the following decades, with keepers withdrawn and their duties transferred to shore control. Some towers were decommissioned, and others were preserved as museums, hotels, or heritage sites, a fate that many of the old stone and iron towers now share. The lighthouse has also become a potent symbol, appearing in art, literature, and popular culture as a figure of guidance, solitude, and the boundary between land and sea. Even as its practical role has narrowed, the lighthouse remains a record of persistent effort: from the Alexandrian fire, through Smeaton's dovetailed granite and Fresnel's glass rings, to the automated beacons that still mark coasts and channels around the world.

Lighthouses are among the oldest deliberate works of navigation, and their history follows the history of the sea itself: the need to bring ships safely past dangerous coasts, and the steady growth of the knowledge needed to do so. The most famous early example was the Pharos of Alexandria, built on the island of Pharos at the entrance to the harbour around 280 BCE, in the reign of Ptolemy II. It was designed by the architect Sostratus of Cnidus, and ancient accounts put its height at somewhere near 100 metres, which would have made it one of the tallest structures in the world for many centuries. A fire burned at its summit, and the light was thought to be visible far out to sea. The Pharos survived for more than a millennium before earthquakes weakened it, and its ruins were finally lost in the early fourteenth century. Its name proved more durable than the building. In Greek, Latin and many modern languages the word for a lighthouse descends from it, as in the Italian *faro*, the French *phare* and the Portuguese *farol*.

The Romans built a number of coastal towers, and a few have survived into the modern era. The best known is the Tower of Hercules at A Coruña in north-west Spain, probably dating from the late first or early second century CE. It is the oldest lighthouse still in use, and it has been restored several times, most recently in the eighteenth century, when its outer casing was rebuilt. Other Roman towers, at Dover and elsewhere along the Channel and the North Sea, served as signal stations or watch towers as much as navigational aids. After the fall of the western empire, the knowledge needed to build such structures became scarce in much of Europe, and for several centuries the guidance of ships relied largely on local knowledge, church bells, and fires lit on headlands or on towers that were built for other purposes. Some medieval harbour towns maintained beacons, and religious houses sometimes kept lights to guide travellers across dangerous crossings, but there was no systematic network.

The modern lighthouse emerged in the early modern period, driven by the growth of maritime trade and the expansion of naval power. The Tour de Cordouan at the mouth of the Gironde in France was begun in 1584 and completed in 1611, and its design, with a richly decorated tower and a lantern at the top, was intended partly as a statement of royal prestige. In Britain the Corporation of Trinity House, chartered by Henry VIII in 1514, gradually took responsibility for marking the coasts, and by the seventeenth century the problem of lighting the most dangerous rocks had become pressing. The Eddystone Rock, some fourteen kilometres off Plymouth, was a notorious hazard, and in 1698 Henry Winstanley built the first lighthouse there on a wooden framework bolted to the rock. Winstanley was a showman and an inventor as well as an engineer, and he was fond of tinkering with his own structure. In November 1703 the Great Storm destroyed the tower, and Winstanley died in it, having gone out to check on its repairs.

The next attempts were more durable. John Rudyerd replaced the wooden structure in 1706 with a tower of timber and stone, which stood for nearly fifty years. Its successor, designed by John Smeaton and completed in 1759, was the most influential structure of its age. Smeaton studied the properties of hydraulic lime, which sets under water, and he shaped the granite blocks so that they interlocked in a form that he compared to the trunk of an oak tree. His tower established principles of construction that engineers relied on for generations, and it stood until the rock beneath it began to erode in the 1870s. The tower was then dismantled and the top portion was re-erected on Plymouth Hoe as a monument. A new lighthouse was built on the rock by James Douglass, and it remains in service today.

Scotland produced an equally remarkable achievement at the Bell Rock, a submerged reef off the coast of Angus that is covered at high tide. Robert Stevenson, a member of the family whose descendants would later include Robert Louis Stevenson, spent years designing and building a tower there between 1807 and 1810. The work was carried out by men who lived in a floating barracks and could only labour during the short windows of low tide. The completed light, first shone in 1811, is still operating, and it stands as a monument to the careful and often dangerous labour that lay behind so many of these structures.

The most significant advance in the technology of the light itself came from France. Before the nineteenth century, lights were typically open fires, then oil lamps with reflectors that threw their output in a fairly diffuse pattern. In 1822 the physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel presented a design for a lens made of concentric rings of glass prisms, which could bend almost all the light from a lamp into a narrow horizontal beam. The lens could be made large and yet remain relatively light, and it allowed a lamp of modest power to be seen from many miles away. The first Fresnel lens was installed at Cordouan in 1823, and the design was rapidly adopted across Europe and the Americas. Lenses were graded by size, with first-order lenses, the largest, being placed on the most important coasts. Some are still in use, though most have now been replaced by modern optics.

Keeping the lights burning was itself a demanding task. Keepers climbed the towers to trim wicks, clean glass, wind clockwork mechanisms that rotated the lenses, and log the weather and the state of the light. Isolated stations were lonely and dangerous, and the keepers faced both the sea and the boredom of long postings with few visitors. The Flannan Isles light in the Outer Hebrides became famous in 1900, when three keepers vanished from the island in December. The relief boat found the lamp still lit and the keepers' meal half prepared, but no trace of the men was ever found, and the disappearance has never been fully explained.

The twentieth century transformed lighthouse keeping. Electricity replaced oil, and the Swedish engineer Gustaf Dalén invented the AGA sun valve in 1912, a device that automatically switched lights on at dusk and off at dawn, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics that year. Automatic lights, radio beacons, and later satellite navigation made the task of guiding ships increasingly independent of the keeper on the rock. Many stations were automated, and the last manned lighthouse in the United States, on Ilwaco in Washington State, was closed to keepers in 1990. Today most lighthouses operate without staff, monitored remotely, and many have been turned into museums, hotels, or sites of local heritage.

The lighthouse thus has a longer history than almost any other engineered structure still in use. It began as a symbol of royal power and commercial ambition, passed through the hands of engineers who learned to build in the open sea, and was transformed by optical physics and then by electrical and automatic control. Its form has changed dramatically, but its purpose has stayed the same: to tell a navigator where the land is, and where the danger lies.

Lighthouses are among the oldest engineered structures people have built for a purpose that remains the same: to tell a sailor where land is. Their history is in part a history of fire, of the fuels and lamps that carried it, and of the optics that eventually made a small flame visible for dozens of miles. It is also a history of stone and mortar set against the sea, and of the administrative bodies that paid for them, lit them, and eventually switched them off.

The most famous early example was the Pharos of Alexandria, built on the small island of Pharos at the entrance to the harbour of the Egyptian city. Construction is usually dated to the reign of Ptolemy II in the early third century BC, and the architect is traditionally given as Sostratus of Cnidus, though the ancient sources that name him are not contemporary. The tower was a massive limestone structure, perhaps between one hundred and one hundred and thirty metres high by most estimates, with a square base, an octagonal middle section, and a cylindrical top. A fire burned at its summit, probably fed by wood or oil, and some ancient writers claimed that a polished metal mirror reflected the light outward, though no surviving description confirms the mechanism. The Pharos became so admired that its name entered several languages as the word for a beacon, and it was counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Earthquakes weakened it over the centuries, and by the fourteenth century its remains had collapsed. Some of its stones were reportedly reused in the fortress that the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay built on the same site.

The Roman world built many lighthouses of its own, and some survive in altered form. The Tower of Hercules at A Coruña, on the northwest coast of Spain, dates to the late first or early second century AD and is the oldest lighthouse still in operation. Its core is a square Roman masonry tower, faced and extended in later centuries, and it still guides ships into a rocky coast. The Romans used lighthouses to mark harbours and dangerous approaches along the Mediterranean and the Atlantic coasts of their provinces, and the surviving examples show a standard method: a tall masonry shaft, a fire at the top, and a stone or brick structure built to withstand both weather and the occasional attack.

After the fall of Rome in the west, the lighthouse tradition thinned out in Europe, though it never disappeared. Coastal communities kept fires burning on headlands and church towers, and religious houses sometimes maintained beacons for pilgrims and merchants. In the Middle Ages, lights were often a local responsibility, supported by tolls, dues on shipping, or the piety of a guild or monastery. Hook Head, on the south coast of Ireland, has a claim to be the oldest operating lighthouse in the English-speaking world, with a tower whose origins go back to the twelfth century, though it has been rebuilt and modernised many times since. In Italy, the Lanterna of Genoa, first recorded in the twelfth century, became a symbol of the city and was rebuilt more than once after damage and fire.

Early modern lighthouses were mostly coal fires. A coal brazier burned in an open iron basket at the top of a tower, and a keeper had to tend it through the night, feed it, and clear the ash. Coal was heavy, smoky, and expensive to carry to remote rocks, and the fire gave a light that was weak, unevenly bright, and easy to confuse with other lights along the same coast. The brazier was also dangerous, since a stray spark could set fire to the lantern room or the wooden fittings that often surrounded it.

The most important early modern development was not in the flame but in the structure beneath it. Rocky reefs far from shore were the places where ships were most often lost, and building on them was difficult. The first Eddystone lighthouse, off Plymouth in England, was a timber structure begun by Henry Winstanley in 1696. It was a fanciful building, decorated with ornamental work, and it lasted only until the great storm of November 1703, when it was swept away with Winstanley himself inside. A second lighthouse, designed by John Rudyerd and built with a more sensible profile of wood and stone, served from 1709 until a fire destroyed it in 1755.

The third Eddystone was the work of John Smeaton, an engineer who had a scientific temperament and a habit of testing materials. Smeaton studied hydraulic lime, a cement that would set under water, and he used the stone and mortar in a new way: the courses of granite were dovetailed and locked together, each block shaped to fit its neighbours, so that the tower behaved more like a single monolith than a stack of separate stones. The lighthouse was completed in 1759 and stood until the rock beneath it was undermined in the late nineteenth century. Its upper part was then taken down and re-erected on Plymouth Hoe, where it still stands as a monument. Smeaton's principles of interlocking masonry and carefully tested lime shaped the designs of many later sea towers, and his work is often treated as the founding moment of modern marine engineering.

The problem of the light itself was addressed in the late eighteenth century. In the 1780s, the Swiss chemist Aimé Argand developed a lamp with a tubular wick and a glass chimney that created a draught, producing a flame that burned brighter and more steadily than a candle or an ordinary oil lamp. Reflectors of polished metal or silvered glass were placed behind the lamps to throw the light outward, and the combination of lamp and reflector was an important step forward. Still, the reflectors had their limits, because they could not capture much of the light that spread in directions away from the observer.

The decisive advance came from the French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel. Working in the 1810s, Fresnel designed a lens built from concentric rings of glass prisms, each ring bending light so that it emerged as a nearly parallel beam. His lens captured far more of the lamp's output than any reflector, and it could be arranged in tiers to form a tall, nearly cylindrical apparatus around the flame. Fresnel's first lenses were installed at the Cordouan lighthouse at the mouth of the Gironde in 1823, and within a few decades such lenses were in use across Europe and in the American colonies and later the United States. The French lighthouse service, and its counterparts elsewhere, adopted the principle of the optic as a standard, and the different lenses were given characteristic arrangements of flashes and eclipses so that a mariner could identify a particular light by its pattern.

The nineteenth century brought a surge of construction, financed by governments, trinity houses, and maritime boards. In Britain, the Trinity House corporation, which had held a royal charter since the sixteenth century, managed a growing network of lights, and engineers such as Robert Stevenson built rock towers far out at sea, including the Bell Rock light off the Scottish coast, completed in 1810 after years of hard work in a tidal reef. Stevenson's family would go on to build a long line of lighthouses around the Scottish coast, and the family's engineering standards became a model. In the United States, the Lighthouse Board, established in 1852, took over the administration of the nation's lights, which had previously been managed in a patchwork of local arrangements. The board standardised equipment, built new towers, and set the pattern for a federal service that would last for more than a century.

Lighthouse keeping was a demanding life. Keepers and their families often lived on remote rocks or islands, cut off from land for weeks at a time by weather. They trimmed wicks, polished lenses, wound clockwork mechanisms that turned the optic, recorded the weather, and sometimes rowed out to rescue shipwrecked sailors. Their logs survive in archives on both sides of the Atlantic and form a valuable record of the work. Many keepers were men with families who depended on a small and uncertain wage. In some services, women served as keepers, and in others the families of keepers took up many of the daily tasks.

The twentieth century changed the trade through technology. Paraffin and then electricity replaced oil and coal as fuels, and vaporised oil and gas lamps spread to outlying lights. Electric lamps, automatic timers, and sealed mechanisms reduced the need for constant human attention. Radio beacons and, later, satellite navigation took over much of the lighthouse's navigational role for large ships, though lights remained important as visual marks and as backups. Through the later decades of the century, most lighthouses in the developed world were automated, and the keepers were withdrawn. Many towers were sold, handed to trusts, or converted into museums, hostels, and private homes, and some of the most remote lights were left to run on solar power and batteries with occasional maintenance visits.

The lighthouse has thus gone through a long arc, from an ancient fire on a harbour island, to Roman masonry on a rocky coast, to the carefully engineered granite of the Eddystone and the glass rings of Fresnel's lens, to the solar-powered automatic lights of the present. The purpose has barely changed in more than two thousand years. What has changed is the means by which a light could be made to reach further, burn more reliably, and tell a sailor exactly where he stood, and the people who built, tended, and eventually stopped tending these towers have left a record that still shapes the coast they once guarded.

Does claude -p --output-format stream-json report the real output-token count?

Question

No doc sentence: a practical bug report. An integration launches claude -p --output-format stream-json --verbose without --include-partial-messages and reads message.usage.output_tokens from the assistant events. It sometimes gets 4 or 6 output tokens for a long answer. Hypothesis: those events carry the usage of the API message_start event, not the final count. The final count only arrives in the API message_delta event, and that event is forwarded (as stream_event) only with --include-partial-messages.

Confirmed if, for every API message (message.id), the assistant events carry a value far below the real one, while with the flag message_delta.usage.output_tokens, summed per message, equals result.usage.output_tokens. Run mode: claude -p only.

Follow-up questions, for a chat that spans several processes (claude -p, then claude -p --resume <id> twice):

  • A. Does each process's result (usage, modelUsage, total_cost_usd) cover that process only, or the conversation so far?
  • B. Once the chat is over, can every token (input, cache, output) be recovered from the session files alone, without having watched the stream?

Why: the assistant event is emitted before message_delta

From the partial-mode timeline (multi-tool-partial-r1.jsonl, ms from start):

  2034 ASSISTANT          …C1Rkp1di tool_use  output_tokens=20  stop_reason=null

  • Claude Code emits one assistant event per content block, when that block ends, so before the API sends message_delta.
    • Each event carries a copy of the usage from message_start. There, output_tokens is only the handful of tokens counted so far (1–20 here).
    • stop_reason is null in every assistant event of all 30 runs.
  • The same partial usage is repeated on every event of a message, and all of them share its message.id.
    • A message with thinking emits two assistant events (thinking, then text). A message with 3 parallel tool calls emits three.
    • Summing over events instead of over message.id therefore doubles or triples that wrong number. That is how a 4000-token essay shows up as 4 or 6: 2 + 2, or 3 + 3.
  • The flag changes nothing in the assistant events: they carry the same partial snapshot in both modes. It only adds the stream_events, among them message_delta. Its usage.output_tokens is the final per-message count.
  • The session transcript .jsonl holds the final count for every message, repeated on each content-block entry. So Claude Code knows the correct value; it just doesn't update the stream event it has already sent.
  • system:thinking_tokens events (estimated_tokens) arrive during thinking in both modes. They are an estimate of thinking only, not a usage count.

  • No provisional values. Every entry of every message carries the same output, with output_tokens_details and a stop_reason. The CAIP-report's premise that "only the line carrying output_tokens_details holds the final figure" does not hold for this session.
  • All 44 calls matched. Each call was paired with the report's callLog on its exact prompt sizes, and the report's estimate is low every time. Three reasons:
    • thinking is excluded (2414 tokens);
    • the p50k_base tokenizer gives 75–81% of the real count on text-only messages;

Each agent-<id> file name is the subagent's task_id, as given in the stream's system:task_started event together with the tool_use_id of the Agent call that started it.

Conclusion

Confirmed. In Claude Code 2.1.327, the assistant.message.usage.output_tokens of claude -p stream-json is the message_start snapshot, never the final count, with or without --include-partial-messages.

Whether you call it a bug or a design limitation, the field is unreliable for output tokens: the event goes out before the API has reported them. The reliable sources:

  1. result.usage.output_tokens (or result.modelUsage): the exact total of the whole -p invocation. It needs no flag. This is the simplest fix when one total per run is enough.
  2. stream_event → message_delta.usage.output_tokens, with --include-partial-messages: exact per API message, in real time.
    • Attribute it to the message.id of the preceding message_start.
    • Take one value per message.
  3. The session transcript, after the fact: exact per message, but deduplicate by message.id.

Whatever the source, never sum usage over assistant events. Group by message.id.

Multi-process chats. Each process's result.usage covers that process only. modelUsage and total_cost_usd are session running totals: take the last one, don't sum them.

Subagents appear in neither result.usage nor the stream's stream_events. At runtime they appear only in the cumulative per-model modelUsage / total_cost_usd. Afterwards they appear exactly in subagents/agent-*.jsonl and in cost-state.

Edge cases.

  • With background subagents one process emits several result events: sum result.usage over all of them.
  • Nested subagents land in the same subagents/ folder.
  • --thinking-display summarized and --forward-subagent-text change nothing.
  • A max_tokens stop is counted exactly, including Claude Code's automatic continuations.
  • The one gap: an API message cut off by killing the process is recorded nowhere, not in the stream, the files or cost-state. Those tokens are lost to any accounting.

Real sessions. In a real 2.1.319 session (main + 2 subagents), the deduplicated file usage is exact and equals cost-state. A CAIP-report built from the same session estimates only 48% of the output tokens. Reading usage.output_tokens per message.id beats tokenizing the text.

Cost per agent. Neither the files nor the stream carry a cost per subagent. Pricing each agent file's deduplicated usage with the list prices reproduces Claude Code's own costUSD exactly, per model and in total, so it is the way to cost each subagent. When subagents share the main session's model, it is the only way.

After the chat is over, the session .jsonl holds everything, with no need to have watched the stream:

  • Per message: the assistant entries, deduplicated by message.id.
  • Per chat: the last cost-state entry (cumulative cost and per-model usage, thinking included).

Not tested

  • Agent SDK (includePartialMessages) and interactive mode.
  • Whether the API bills the tokens of a message cut off by a kill (the session records nothing of them). A kill that hits a subagent mid-message. Prices above 100K-token prompts (Haiku 5.5's higher tier), fast mode, and models other than Haiku 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5 in the cost check. Also --input-format stream-json.
  • --fork-session, --continue, and a --resume run after compaction.
  • Other models and effort levels.
  • Runs that hit max_tokens or are interrupted, where message_delta or result may be missing.
  • Input and cache fields in the first batch: only output_tokens was compared there. The resume run compares all four fields.

Does a launching subagent wait for its nested background subagent?

Claim under test, from https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents#let-subagents-spawn-their-own-subagents:

In an interactive session ... a subagent that launches background subagents waits for their results before it finishes. In non-interactive mode and the Agent SDK, the launching subagent doesn't wait, so a nested background subagent that finishes after its launcher has ended reports to your main conversation instead.

Two follow-ups use the same harness: whether N foreground subagents run in parallel when main spawns them in one message, and whether resuming a completed subagent with SendMessage is sync or async for main.

Setup

main (SDK query or claude -p)  --Agent-->  launcher  --Agent-->  slow-worker

Fixture (this folder):

  • .claude/agents/launcher.md: its only tool is Agent. It spawns one slow-worker, then ends its turn right away with LAUNCHER_FINAL: <token or NO_WORKER_RESULT_YET>. With no other tools it cannot wait on its own, so any waiting you see comes from the harness, not from the model.
  • .claude/agents/slow-worker.md: its only tool is Bash. It runs a 40 s Node timer that prints a random WORKER_TOKEN=<n>. Only the worker knows the token, so if the token shows up somewhere, the worker's result got there.
  • .claude/agents/resumable.md: draws a hidden NONCE on its first run and ends with FIRST_RUN_DONE; when resumed with CONTINUE it waits 20 s and returns RESUMED_FINAL NONCE=<n>.
  • prompts/: the main prompts, rendered by the drivers. nested-main.md (experiment.ts, nested-cli.ts), parallel-main.md (parallel.ts, parallel-cli.ts), resume-main.md (resume.ts). prompts/parallel-fanout.md is the reusable fan-out instruction distilled from the parallel results; no driver reads it.

Drivers (this folder; the shared harness is lib/claude-home.mjs):

  • experiment.ts runs main through the TypeScript Agent SDK:
    • A PreToolUse hook on Agent sets run_in_background for each scenario. It also records whether the model had already chosen that value; in every run it had.
    • SubagentStart, SubagentStop, and PostToolUse hooks, plus the task_started, task_notification, task_updated, and background_tasks_changed stream events, give the timestamps.
    • The prompt is streaming input that stays open until all background work has finished (open), is closed after the first result (close), or is a plain string (string, the 1shot-* scenarios).
  • nested-cli.ts: the same one-shot matrix through the installed claude -p, with command hooks logging to <run>.hooks.jsonl. Sync/async comes from the prompt alone; no hook changes any input.
  • parallel.ts / parallel-cli.ts: main is asked to emit N slow-worker Agent calls in one message. Foreground is forced by CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1 and CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0.
  • resume.ts: main spawns resumable with run_in_background: false, then resumes the same instance with SendMessage to its agentId. forced sets the two variables above; default sets none.

Scenarios are named outer-inner. outer is how main spawns the launcher and inner is how the launcher spawns the worker; fg means foreground and bg means background. direct-* has main spawn the worker itself.

Result

The claim is true for the Agent SDK and for claude -p.

  • Inner background (fg-bg, bg-bg): the launcher ended at about 5–6 s with NO_WORKER_RESULT_YET. Its SubagentStop reported 1 background task still in flight, and the harness never woke it again (one stop only). The worker finished at about 52 s. Its task_notification was delivered to the main conversation as an injected turn (result.origin.kind = "task-notification"), and main reported the token.
  • Inner foreground (fg-fg, bg-fg): the launcher's Agent call blocked until the worker finished, and the launcher's final message contains the token. This is the expected foreground behavior and acts as the control.
  • How main spawns the launcher (fg or bg) made no difference to whether the launcher waited.

Main conversation

results/<run>/<scenario>.main-transcript.txt holds what the main model was actually fed, taken from the session transcript.

  • Launcher in the foreground: main's Agent call blocks until the launcher ends, then main ends its turn. Main waits for the launcher only, never for the background worker.
  • Launcher in the background: main's Agent call returns Async agent launched immediately. Main ends its turn while the launcher is still running.
  • Notification turns: every background subagent that finishes later, including the nested worker, is injected into main as a new user turn. The turn holds a <task-notification> block with <result>...</result> and has origin.kind = "task-notification", and it produces its own result message.
  • main-busy: the worker finished while main was still inside its own 70 s command. The notification was queued (a queued_command attachment) and folded into main's current turn after the command returned. There was no separate turn: one result answered both the prompt and the notification. (In the rerun main's answer carried only the MAIN_GOT_NOTIFICATION line, not also MAIN_TURN_DONE; the delivery was the same.)
  • main-close / main-string: closing the input after the first result, or using a plain string prompt, did not kill the worker. The CLI stayed alive until the worker finished, ran the notification turn, emitted a second result, and only then ended the query() iterator, at about 54 s.

Does the WORKER_TOKEN reach main before the session ends? (1shot-* scenarios)

These scenarios use a plain string prompt, so nothing in the script holds the session open. Every chain was tested: direct, and through the launcher, with each sync/async combination. In all of them the CLI stayed alive until the worker finished, main received the token, and only then did the session end, about 0.3 s after main's last answer.

  • Sync all the way (main →fg worker, main →fg launcher →fg worker): the token comes back in the prompt's own turn, as the return value of the Agent call. There is a single result.
  • Any async link in the chain: main's prompt turn ends with NONE. The token arrives later in a task-notification turn, with a separate result per notification:
    • When the launcher is async and the worker is sync, the token comes inside the launcher's notification.
    • When the worker is async, the token comes in the worker's own notification, delivered straight to main and bypassing the launcher, which has already ended.

Headless claude -p vs the SDK (nested-cli.ts, parallel-cli.ts)

Behaviour is identical:

  • With an async worker, the launcher doesn't wait.
  • The worker's callback goes to main, never to the launcher.
  • The process stays alive until every callback has been handled.
  • Each chain delivered the token the same way (sync or callback).

One stream difference: in -p mode every result line is held back until all background work has finished, then all of them are written together just before exit. Main's answer text still streams live when it is written. The SDK emits each result as soon as its turn ends.

Parallel foreground fan-out (parallel.ts, parallel-cli.ts)

With 5 workers, in both runs of both drivers: main emitted all 5 Agent calls in one message, all ran in the foreground, the workers started within about 1.5 s of each other and finished in about 48–50 s of wall time (against about 240 s of summed worker time), and main had all 5 tokens before it answered.

Resuming a completed sync subagent: sync or async for main? (resume.ts)

env what SendMessage returns how main gets the resumed run's reply verdict
forced (CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1, CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0) blocks ~22–23 s, then Resumed agent. Its final report follows… + the report inline, as the tool result; a single result SYNC
default (no env vars) returns in under 0.25 s with Resuming agent <id>, resumedAgentId main ends its turn ("waiting…"); the report arrives later as a <task-notification> turn and gets a second result ASYNC

The same pattern held for the SDK and for claude -p. In every run the resumed subagent was the same instance: one transcript, and the nonce matched. A SendMessage resume ignores how the subagent was first spawned. It runs in the background, as the docs say, unless background tasks are disabled. The task_started event for the resume reports is_backgrounded: true in both modes. SendMessage is a deferred tool, so main first loads it with ToolSearch.

Conclusion

In the Agent SDK and in claude -p, a subagent that launches a background subagent does not wait for it: the launcher ends, and the nested subagent's result is delivered to the main conversation as a task-notification turn. The session stays alive until that delivery has happened, even with a one-shot prompt. Foreground subagents spawned in one message run in parallel, and a SendMessage resume is async unless background tasks are disabled. Confirmed on Claude Code 2.1.296 (SDK and -p) and 2.1.299 (-p).

Not tested

The interactive-mode half of the claim, where the launcher does wait. That needs an interactive terminal session (node lib/claude-home.mjs investigations/subagent-background-behaviour).

The glossary is wrong on two counts. The syntax is @path, not @import path (the latter did nothing in any file). And the import is not limited to CLAUDE.md: it also works in CLAUDE.local.md, .claude/rules/*.md and sub-directory CLAUDE.md (relative to the importing file), and in skill and slash-command bodies and the user prompt (relative to cwd). It does not work in subagent bodies or in files read with Read; AGENTS.md could not be judged. Nesting works, cycles are harmless, code spans and code blocks are skipped, and the chain stopped after four levels, which matches the documented limit of four hops. Everything the docs state about @path was confirmed; the runs add the carriers the docs do not mention. All of this holds for Claude Code 2.1.328 in claude -p, one run per scenario.

Can the input tokens of a claude -p conversation be split into tool results, user messages, skills/instructions and preamble pieces?

Question

No doc sentence: a practical question. Every API call reports one prompt size (input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + cache_read_input_tokens). Is there any way to see how much of it is:

  • tool results,
  • user messages,
  • skills and instructions (CLAUDE.md, skill listing, skill body),
  • the preamble, itemized (system prompt, tool definitions, …)?

Sources: the stdout of claude -p --output-format stream-json --verbose without and with --include-partial-messages, and the session .jsonl, read at the end or during the conversation.

Confirmed if some source gives a per-category token figure, or a method reconstructs it so that the parts add up to the call's prompt size. Refuted if no source has per-block counts and no method gets close. Run mode: claude -p only (agreed with the user), on Haiku 5.5.

Follows stream-json-output-tokens, which settled the per-message totals; this one is about what is inside the input side.

cwd = fixtures/<name>/   (GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES is set but did not stop git: the prompt still carries the repo's git status. It was constant during the batch, hence the identical sizes.)

It records per API call the usage from every source (assistant event, message_start, message_delta, session file) and every numeric "token" field of the stream and the session file. Output: runs.json.

  • fixtures/, regenerated by the driver on every run: empty; claudemd-w200/-w800 (a CLAUDE.md of 200 / 800 words); skills-1/-3 (1 or 3 skills with 800-word bodies); skillbody-w200/-w800 (one skill, invoked); tooldata (files of 100 / 800 words and a tiny one, read with cat). All text is plain deterministic English with a marker string, so tokens per word are comparable across categories.
  • prompts/: reply-ok, user-filler (padding + "reply OK"), invoke-skill, run-bash. Each scenario makes 1 or 2 API calls per process, deterministic.
  • Added later: tool-parallel (prompt run-bash-parallel: cat tiny.txt, cat data-w100.txt and cat data-w800.txt as three parallel Bash calls in one message).
  • Added later: the MCP scenarios (mcp-base, mcp-tiny, mcp-w100, mcp-w800, mcp-parallel). datamcp.mjs is a stdio MCP server with one tool, lookup, that returns the text of the same data files as the Bash scenarios (tiny, 100 words, 800 words), and sends 278 characters of server instructions. The run uses --mcp-config fixtures/mcp.json --strict-mcp-config; prompts run-mcp and run-mcp-parallel.
  • Scenario groups: user (base, 200 and 800 padding words), instructions (CLAUDE.md sizes), skills (listing of 1 / 3 skills, never invoked; invocation with 200 / 800-word body), tool-result (tiny, 100, 800 words), user-multi (turn 1 short, turn 2 200 words, turn 3 800 words, one session), preamble (leave-one-out with --tools "", --tools Bash, --tools Bash,Read, --disable-slash-commands, --system-prompt, --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections, and several together as a floor).

  • count-tokens.ts: added after the first batch. It rebuilds each request from the session file (system blocks and tool definitions from api-request-shape, messages from api-request-blob and the session entries) and counts pieces and whole requests with POST /v1/messages/count_tokens. There is no API key here, so it authenticates with the run's OAuth token (Authorization: Bearer + anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20, plus the advisor / inline-tools betas the tool definitions need). It sends only text from the fixtures' session files; the first user message also carries the account email and git status, which Claude Code itself sends in every call.
  • Ground truth: differences between scenarios that change one thing, the growth of the prompt between consecutive calls (P(n+1) − P(n) − output(n)), and the independent count_tokens figures.

Result

1. No source has a per-category token figure

Every numeric field with "token" in its name, over all 138 runs, stream and session files: the only fields that are not totals are system:thinking_tokens.estimated_tokens (a running estimate of thinking only), cache_miss_reason.cache_missed_input_tokens (present only on a cache miss) and max_tokens (a request limit). Everything else is input / cache_creation / cache_read / output / thinking per API call, modelUsage and the cost-state entry. Nothing is split by tool result, user message, skill or system block.

The session file does contain the text of every piece: api-request-shape (system blocks and tool definitions), api-request-blob, skill_listing, prompt_snapshot, instructions, and the user entries with their tool_results. It has characters, not tokens.

2. With and without --include-partial-messages

The input side of every call is complete and final in the assistant event, with or without the flag. The flag adds stream_events only: message_start carries the same usage earlier (before the first block), and message_delta the final output. It adds no per-category information. So the attribution below works from either mode; the session file gives it after the fact.

3. Attribution from consecutive calls and from scenario differences

The prompt size per scenario is deterministic (spread 0 over 6 runs; only the cache_creation / cache_read split moves), so differences are exact. Tokens per word: user message 2.06; CLAUDE.md 2.13; tool result 2.14; skill body 2.09: one slope for one text type.

5. Surprise: connector instructions arrive mid-conversation, nondeterministically

Without --strict-mcp-config, the second call of a tool-using session is 3743 tokens larger than the same session with it (a mcp_instructions_delta attachment appears in the session file). A naive "growth = tool result" would blame the tool result. In the multi-turn scenario the same jump appeared at turn 2 of the partial run (28969 vs 25226) but not in the plain run of the same rep, so the timing depends on when the connectors finish connecting. The 2 plain/partial differences of Result 2 are exactly these. The attribution is exact only if each growth is cross-checked against the attachments the session file records for that call.

8. MCP tool results, and what an MCP server costs besides its results

One stdio server, one tool (mcp__datamcp__lookup), 3 reps per scenario, partial mode (the plain runs give the same prompt sizes).

  • The tool is deferred. Its definition is not in the first request: only its name is in the deferred_tools_delta list, and the server's instructions arrive as an mcp_instructions_delta attachment. The first call is 24848 tokens, 146 more than without the server; the instructions alone (278 chars) count 95 tokens.
  • Every MCP use took 3 API calls, not 2: (1) the model calls ToolSearch with select:mcp__datamcp__lookup, the result is a tool_reference and Claude Code records the loaded definition (deferred_tools_record); (2) the model calls lookup; (3) the answer. The extra call re-reads the whole ≈ 25k prompt (from cache). Growth from call 1 to call 2 is 249 tokens: 86 are call 1's output, 163 are the ToolSearch result with the tool definition and the per-call reminder.
  • Thinking comes back as input. In 3 of 12 runs call 1 contained a thinking block (output 114–152 instead of 86). In those runs growth 1→2 is 283–315, so "growth − call 1 output" is 163 in all 12 runs: the whole output, thinking included, re-enters in the next prompt.
  • The lookup result follows the same rule as Bash. Results counted alone: 15 / 230 / 1726 tokens for the tiny, 100-word and 800-word notes (Bash: 14 / 229 / 1725). The lookup round as counted (tool_use + results) is 79, 293 and 1789 tokens for one lookup, and 2248 for three parallel lookups. Usage growth from call 2 to call 3 is exactly counted + 24 in all 12 runs, as with Bash.
  • Output of an MCP call: 57–58 tokens for the lookup tool_use, 166 for three parallel ones, final values from the session file or message_delta.

9. Avoiding the extra ToolSearch round: ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false

Scenarios eager-mcp-base and eager-mcp-w100: same server, same prompts, with ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false in the process environment, 3 reps × 2 modes.

For one small MCP tool that is a worse trade: two calls of about 44k against three of about 25k. The 44k prefix is also a new cache entry, so its first call wrote it (cache_creation 43847) instead of reading it. It could pay off with many MCP tools used in most sessions; this run does not show where the break-even is.

Conclusion

Native itemization: refuted. Attribution: confirmed, by calculation and by counting the text in the log.

  • No field of stream-json (with or without --include-partial-messages) or of the session .jsonl holds tokens per tool result, user message, skill, instruction or preamble block. Only totals per API call (input, cache, output, thinking), per model, and cost.
  • The flag does not help here: the input side of each call is the same, and available at the same moment (the assistant event, or message_start a little earlier), in both modes. The session file gives the same figures afterwards.
  • Tool results, user messages, skill bodies and CLAUDE.md can be attributed exactly per call from the growth of the prompt between consecutive calls (minus the previous output), on this version, with linear scaling and equal slope across categories. The session file shows which block entered between two calls (user entry, tool_result, attachment). The fixed overhead of a block (≈ 44 for a tool result, ≈ 70 for a later user turn, ≈ 197 for CLAUDE.md) is not separable from the content without a second measurement.
  • The preamble can be itemized in tokens from one finished conversation: the session file holds the text of every piece, and counting it with count_tokens reproduces the first call's prompt size to within 2 tokens of 24702. Without count_tokens, leave-one-out runs with flags give the same split within 0.2%; a chars-to-tokens ratio does not, because it varies by content (0.31 to 0.50).
  • A rebuilt request misses any message the session file does not record as a plain entry (here the skill body, 1789 tokens): the residual against the usage figure is the check.
  • Per tool call: the output is the final output_tokens of the API message that emitted it (shared among its parallel calls: 250–253 for three); the input is the growth to the next call, minus that output where it re-enters, minus ≈ 24 of per-call reminder, and for parallel calls it must be split by counting each result.
  • MCP: the results follow the same rules as built-in tools. What differs is the cost around them: instructions (95 tokens here), the deferred name list, one extra ToolSearch round (≈ 163 tokens of growth and one more API call over the whole prompt), and the result wrapped as a text content block (no measurable extra). Thinking output re-enters as input.
  • Check the attachments of each call (mcp_instructions_delta, deferred_tools_delta, skill_listing): content that Claude Code adds by itself lands in the same growth.

Not tested

  • Interactive mode, and the Agent SDK.
  • count_tokens with a real API key (the OAuth route worked here, but it is not a documented public path), later turns of long sessions, and per-block counts of the user-turn overhead in the multi-turn scenarios.
  • Other models: all runs are Haiku 5.5, whose tokenizer may differ from others. Claude Code 2.1.328 only.
  • More than three parallel calls, errors and truncated results.
  • Other ways to reduce the repeated prompt (a shorter CLAUDE.md, fewer tools with --tools, keeping the cache warm, TTL), and the break-even of ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH with many MCP tools.
  • MCP: one server with one small tool over stdio. Not tested: several servers or many tools (when Claude Code stops deferring or starts truncating), large structured or image results, resources and prompts, HTTP/SSE servers, the claude.ai connectors' own tools.
  • Images and PDFs, subagent transcripts, compaction and context-management edits, which change the prompt without a new block. Only text, Bash and Skill were used.
  • Whether thinking blocks of earlier turns (not earlier calls of the same turn) stay in the prompt. Within a turn they do (Result 8).
  • The effect of the cache on the split: only the sum was used.

<!-- A labelled grid rather than a run-on line, so every figure states what it measures. The rule

# Parallel fan-out instruction (reusable)

## Standing rule (for CLAUDE.md or any agent's instructions)

A conditional rule that sits next to the task- or workspace-specific instructions and only applies when the
agent decides to delegate. It works for the main agent and for any subagent that has the Agent tool.

```text
## Spawning subagents
If you need more than one subagent and their subtasks do not depend on each other's results:
- Spawn them all in the same response: one Agent tool call per subagent, all in that single response.
  Do not spawn them one response at a time.
- Run them in the foreground (run_in_background: false, when the option exists) if you need their results
  before you continue. Calls made in the same response still run in parallel.
- Give each subagent a self-contained prompt: it cannot see this conversation.
- Wait for all of their results before you continue, then combine them.
If a subtask needs another subtask's output, spawn those one after the other instead.
```

## Explicit fan-out block

Drop this block into any agent's instructions: the main prompt, a system prompt, or the body of a
`.claude/agents/*.md` subagent that is allowed to spawn its own subagents. Replace the `{{…}}` placeholders.

```text
## Parallel delegation
When you delegate the subtasks below, run them in parallel and wait for all of them:
1. Spawn all {{N}} subagents in ONE single response: that one response contains {{N}} Agent tool calls and
   nothing else. Do not send them one per response, and do not wait for one to finish before calling the next.
2. Run every call in the foreground: if the Agent tool offers run_in_background, set it to false.
   You need every result before you continue.
3. One call per subtask:
{{SUBTASKS}}
   Give each call its own short description (for example "<task name> <k>"), and put everything the
   subagent needs into its prompt: it does not see this conversation.
4. Continue only after all {{N}} results are back. If a call fails, say which one and why; do not retry it
   unless told to.
5. Then {{WHAT_TO_DO_WITH_THE_RESULTS}}.
```

## Filled-in example (what the 5-worker test does)

```text
## Parallel delegation
When you delegate the subtasks below, run them in parallel and wait for all of them:
1. Spawn all 5 subagents in ONE single response: that one response contains 5 Agent tool calls and
   nothing else. Do not send them one per response, and do not wait for one to finish before calling the next.
2. Run every call in the foreground: if the Agent tool offers run_in_background, set it to false.
   You need every result before you continue.
3. One call per subtask:
   - k = 1..5: subagent_type "slow-worker", prompt "Run your task."
   Give each call its own short description (for example "slow worker <k>"), and put everything the
   subagent needs into its prompt: it does not see this conversation.
4. Continue only after all 5 results are back. If a call fails, say which one and why; do not retry it
   unless told to.
5. Then end your turn with one line: MAIN_TURN_DONE: followed by every WORKER_TOKEN=... line you received.
```

## Using it in a subagent that spawns its own subagents

- The subagent needs the `Agent` tool: list it in `tools`, or omit `tools` to inherit everything.
- It must be above the depth limit. `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH` defaults to 3 layers; at the limit
  Claude Code removes `Agent` and the subagent does the work itself.
- Foreground is the default only when Claude asks for it. To guarantee it for the whole session, set
  `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS=1` (and `CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0`). In that case step 2 is
  redundant but harmless.
- The total number of subagents running at once counts against `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS`
  (default 20) across every layer.

Does a subagent read, on demand and by direct path, the reference files named in its body?

+ +

Question

+

Claim under test (no doc sentence; it comes from the user's design idea): a subagent defined as .claude/agents/architect/architect.md can name files in its body, such as .claude/agents/architect/references/xxx.md, with "read xxx.md for more information". The subagent then reads them only when needed, by going straight to the path, without scanning the directory. Their content is not preloaded into its context, unlike an Agent Skill, whose description is always loaded.

+

Confirmed if the subagent's first tool call for a needed file is a Read that succeeds (no Glob, Grep or ls/find before it), if the file's NONCE is not in the subagent transcript before its first tool call, and if unneeded files are never read. Refuted if it has to scan, or if the content is already there without a Read. Run mode: claude -p only (no Agent SDK, no interactive).

+ +

Setup

+
claude -p (cwd = this folder) --Agent--> architect (tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash) --Read--> references/<topic>.md
+
    +
  • .claude/agents/architect/architect.md: the body names references/naming.md, layering.md, security.md with paths relative to the agent file. Scanning tools are allowed on purpose, so a scan would show up.
    • +
  • .claude/agents/architect-rooted/architect-rooted.md: control. Same shape, but the body writes the paths from the project root (.claude/agents/architect-rooted/references/…).
    • +
  • references/*.md in each agent folder: one line of content plus an unguessable NONCE=<n> each, different between the two agents.
    • +
  • prompts/main.md: the main prompt, a strict script: call the Agent once, repeat its answer.
    • +
  • reference-files-cli.ts: spawns the installed claude -p with stream-json, collects the subagent's tool calls (events with parent_tool_use_id), judges them and checks the first lines of the subagent transcript for preloaded NONCEs.
    • +
  • Scenarios: rel-naming (1 file needed, relative path), rooted-naming (control), rel-two (2 of 3 files needed), rel-none (no file needed). Model: sonnet. Env: ISOLATION_ENV from lib/claude-home.mjs.
    • +
+ +

Run

+
node lib/claude-home.mjs investigations/subagent-reference-files --check
+npx tsx investigations/subagent-reference-files/reference-files-cli.ts [rel-naming rooted-naming rel-two rel-none]
+

Session logs: .claude-home/projects/sessions/<session-id>.jsonl, subagent transcripts under <session-id>/subagents/.

Author: Samuele Pesce <spesce@codearchitects.com>
Date:   Wed Nov 18 13:17:24 2026 +0100

    Add stream-json-output-tokens investigation (claude -p)
    
    Output tokens in claude -p stream-json and in the session files:
    - assistant events carry the message_start usage (provisional output), with or
      without --include-partial-messages; message_delta, result and the session
      .jsonl (dedup by message.id) are exact
    - --resume: result.usage is per process, modelUsage/total_cost_usd cumulative;
      the session file's cost-state holds the running totals
    - subagents: not in result.usage nor stream_events; exact in
      subagents/agent-*.jsonl and cost-state; per-agent cost recomputed exactly
    - edge cases: killed processes, flags, background/nested subagents, max_tokens
    - a real 2.1.319 session vs its CAIP-report: report estimates 48% of output
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

      and REPORT.html; CLAUDE.md documents the layout and workflow.
